reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that motion perception involves a dual process: active innervation of the eye to resist environmental drag, and selective assignment of visual components to background or foreground. Retinal innervation creates a mechanical basis for perceived motion, while background assignment determines which component is interpreted as moving. This duality leads to illusions such as the riverboat effect where the river appears to move despite stationary observation. The model assumes that the brain computes relative motion using a weighted sum of visual inputs, where attention biases the assignment of motion to specific components. When attention focuses on a moving pattern (e.g., oilcloth), it becomes the perceived reference frame, causing other elements to appear stationary. Conversely, when attention shifts to the environment, the pattern appears to move. This mechanism underlies both the illusion and its resolution, suggesting a Bayesian framework where prior beliefs about motion are updated based on sensory input and attentional weighting. The breakdown occurs when these assignments fail due to conflicting sensory signals or attentional interference.
